rows.description: A toddler asks what-that with rising tone or a pointing gesture, seeking names and attention. The question is often social as much as informational, so an answer plus a smile is enough.
A preschooler's repeated why questions signal curiosity, wanting attention or testing limits. Short honest answers or asking what the child thinks keep the dialogue alive without exhaustion.
A child asks a friend are you okay when noticing sad or quiet behaviour. Kind inquiry shows care, and the friend may or may not want to answer yet.

rows.subtype: Worry showing as stomach aches and clinging [Actor]
rows.description: A child complains of aches before school, cries at separation and asks many what if questions. The body feels the fear, and calm routines and gentle steps toward the feared thing help.

A teenager feels tense, cannot sleep and spirals over grades, health or friends, and may seem irritable. It is more than ordinary nerves when it lasts and limits life, and calls for talking to a counsellor.
A young adult in a new city or job feels racing thoughts, tight chest and fear of not coping, yet hides it. Sharing with someone and seeking professional help early is a strength, not weakness.

A bright child stumbles over words, reverses letters and hides books, and starts to think they are stupid. Intelligence is intact; reading is the hard part, and early help and patience protect confidence.

A teenager may think in pictures, tell stories brilliantly and struggle with spelling and reading speed under time limits. Getting an assessment and permitted accommodations shows what they truly know.
A young adult uses audio books, voice tools and extra time, and feels embarrassed at first to ask. Sharing the difference with tutors and employers usually earns understanding and shows real ability.

rows.subtype: Big feelings in a small body [Actor]
rows.description: A toddler screams with joy or falls to the floor in rage over small things and cannot yet calm alone. Intensity is a temperament, and calm adult presence is the way children learn to settle.
A teenager feels intense crushes, rage at unfairness and deep sadness, sometimes within one day. Hormones and a developing brain amplify emotion; it is often normal but needs steady adults.
A young adult gives all to friendships and causes and also gets overwhelmed and exhausted. Learning to ride waves, choose the timing of hard talks and keep routines supports depth without collapse.

rows.subtype: Feeling like a fraud in a top college [Actor]
rows.description: A student admitted to a prestigious institute believes they got in by luck and that everyone will soon find out; success is discounted while comparison with others is harsh.

rows.subtype: Working overly hard to avoid exposure [Actor]
rows.description: A new employee stays late and over-prepares because they fear being seen as unqualified; the cycle of effort and relief keeps the belief alive since success is credited to overwork.
A wise writer produces a rough draft without judging, leaves it for a while and then edits with fresh eyes. Separating creating from editing prevents both blank-page fear and endless polishing.
A skilled writer states the point first, uses short sentences, gives dates and numbers, and ends with the exact action needed. Reading it aloud and cutting a third usually improves it.
